Title: Humans, AI, and Context: Understanding End-Users' Trust in a Real-World Computer Vision Application
Authors: Sunnie S. Y. Kim; Elizabeth Anne Watkins; Olga Russakovsky; Ruth Fong; Andres Monroy-Hernandez
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2023 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT '23), pp. 77-88
Problem addressed: Lab studies of AI trust miss how real end-users trust a deployed CV app in context.
Target population: 20 real end-users of a popular AI bird-identification app.
Main findings: Users generally found the app trustworthy, yet accepted outputs selectively after verification and avoided it in high-stakes situations; domain knowledge and context shaped trust.
Research gaps: Little work on trust when the AI user (caregiver) is different from the person affected by errors (blind user).
Relevance to SPARSH: SPARSH's caregiver is exactly this 'verifying' end-user; errors propagate to a blind person who cannot easily verify visually -> higher stakes.
Design implications: Design for verification (side-by-side photo with numbered boxes), make low-confidence detections salient, and treat the final mapping as a high-stakes confirmation step.

Title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
Authors: John D. Lee; Katrina A. See
Problem addressed: People misuse or disuse imperfect automation when trust does not match capability.
Methodology: Integrative review across organisational, sociological, interpersonal, psychological and neurological perspectives; conceptual model.
Main findings: Trust should be calibrated to capability, have good resolution and functional/temporal specificity; convey purpose, process and performance in forms that match how trust forms; realistic/polished displays can inflate trust without improving accuracy.
Relevance to SPARSH: Theoretical basis for showing per-switch detection confidence (specificity) instead of a single global accuracy.
Design implications: Show confidence per detection; explain what the detector does and its known failure modes (e.g., reflections, dual switches); avoid over-polished UI that implies certainty.

Title: Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse
Problem addressed: Characterising how humans use automation inappropriately.
Main findings: Defines use, misuse (over-reliance; missed failures, biased decisions), disuse (neglect, e.g., due to false alarms) and abuse (automating without regard to human performance).
Relevance to SPARSH: Frames SPARSH risks: caregiver misuse (rubber-stamping detections) and disuse (ignoring CV after early errors).
Design implications: Measure both errors accepted (misuse) and correct detections overridden (disuse) in evaluation.

Title: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction
Authors: Saleema Amershi; Dan Weld; Mihaela Vorvoreanu; Adam Fourney; Besmira Nushi; Penny Collisson; Jina Suh; Shamsi Iqbal; Paul N. Bennett; Kori Inkpen; Jaime Teevan; Ruth Kikin-Gil; Eric Horvitz
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '19), pp. 1-13
Problem addressed: Lack of validated, general guidance for designing AI-infused products.
Methodology: Synthesis of guidelines and multiple rounds of evaluation incl. user study with practitioners.
Main findings: 18 generally applicable guidelines validated (individual guideline wording not verified from fetched pages).
Limitations: Guideline text not verified here; consumer-product focus.
Relevance to SPARSH: Standard design framework for SPARSH's caregiver app (expectations, correction, uncertainty).
Design implications: Map SPARSH screens to the 18 guidelines in the report (team should quote guideline wording from the paper itself).

Title: Effect of Confidence and Explanation on Accuracy and Trust Calibration in AI-assisted Decision Making
Authors: Yunfeng Zhang; Q. Vera Liao; Rachel K. E. Bellamy
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAT* '20), pp. 295-305
Problem addressed: Does case-specific information (confidence, explanation) help people trust AI when right and distrust when wrong?
Target population: Participants in two online experiments (n not verified).
Methodology: Two human-subject experiments, AI and humans of comparable accuracy.
Technology: Classifier with confidence scores and local explanations.
Main findings: Showing per-prediction confidence improved trust calibration; but calibration alone did not improve joint accuracy - human needs unique knowledge to catch errors; local explanations were problematic.
Limitations: Abstract-level detail; task was not CV.
Relevance to SPARSH: Direct evidence for SPARSH's per-switch confidence display; caregiver has unique knowledge (knows which switch runs the fan) - the condition under which human+AI can outperform AI.
Design implications: Show confidence per detected switch; explicitly ask caregiver to supply function knowledge the AI cannot have.

Title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
Authors: Gagan Bansal; Tongshuang Wu; Joyce Zhou; Raymond Fok; Besmira Nushi; Ece Kamar; Marco Tulio Ribeiro; Daniel Weld
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2021 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '21), pp. 1-16
Problem addressed: Do explanations help human-AI teams beat both human and AI alone?
Target population: Crowd participants across three datasets (n not verified).
Methodology: Mixed-method user studies with AI of accuracy comparable to humans.
Main findings: AI assistance gave complementary gains, but explanations did not add to them and increased acceptance of AI recommendations even when wrong.
Relevance to SPARSH: Warns that adding 'explanations' (e.g., heatmaps) in SPARSH may increase rubber-stamping.
Design implications: Prefer simple confidence + visual box overlay over elaborate explanations; test acceptance of seeded wrong detections.

Title: To Trust or to Think: Cognitive Forcing Functions Can Reduce Overreliance on AI in AI-assisted Decision-making
Authors: Zana Bucinca; Maja Barbara Malaya; Krzysztof Z. Gajos
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 5(CSCW1), 1-21
Problem addressed: People accept wrong AI suggestions; explanations do not fix it.
Methodology: Experiment comparing three cognitive forcing interventions vs simpler XAI.
Main findings: Cognitive forcing significantly reduced overreliance but was rated least favourably; benefit larger for people high in Need for Cognition.
Limitations: Online task; trade-off with user preference.
Relevance to SPARSH: Justifies a lightweight forcing step in SPARSH (e.g., caregiver must tap each switch to confirm, or physically toggle it, before export).
Design implications: Use a 'confirm each switch by toggling it' step for low-confidence items only, to balance effort and accuracy.

Title: Explanations Can Reduce Overreliance on AI Systems During Decision-Making
Authors: Helena Vasconcelos; Matthew Jorke; Madeleine Grunde-McLaughlin; Tobias Gerstenberg; Michael S. Bernstein; Ranjay Krishna
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 7(CSCW1), 1-38
Problem addressed: Why explanations sometimes fail to reduce overreliance.
Methodology: Maze task with simulated AI; manipulations of task difficulty, explanation difficulty, payment; Cognitive Effort Discounting paradigm.
Main findings: People strategically weigh the cost of verifying vs relying; overreliance drops when verification is made cheap.
Relevance to SPARSH: Key design lever for SPARSH: make verifying a detection cheap (overlay boxes on the photo, one-tap correct).
Design implications: Minimise verification cost: numbered boxes overlaid on the original image, zoom, one-tap add/delete/renumber.

Title: When (ish) is My Bus? User-centered Visualizations of Uncertainty in Everyday, Mobile Predictive Systems
Authors: Matthew Kay; Tara Kola; Jessica R. Hullman; Sean A. Munson
Journal/conference: Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '16), pp. 5092-5103
Problem addressed: How to show prediction uncertainty to lay users on small screens.
Target population: Users of a real-time transit app (survey) and experiment participants (n not verified).
Main findings: Quantile dotplots reduced variance of users' probability estimates (~1.15x vs density plots) and increased confidence.
Relevance to SPARSH: Supports discrete, simple uncertainty encodings for non-expert caregivers.
Design implications: Encode confidence as discrete levels (high / check / low) with colour + text, not raw decimals.
